name: Treaty with the Flatheads, etc., 1855 (Hellgate Treaty)
aka: Treaty with the Flathead, Kootenay, and Upper Pend d'Oreilles, 1855
promises: Article 2 reserved the Jocko (Flathead) reservation for the confederated tribes' exclusive use and benefit, closed to white residents without permission.

Article 3 secured the exclusive right of taking fish in streams through or bordering the reservation, fishing at all usual and accustomed places in common with citizens, and hunting, gathering and pasturing on open and unclaimed land.
Article 4: $120,000 for the cession, part for removal and the rest in annual payments.
Article 11: the Bitterroot Valley above the Lolo Fork was to be surveyed and could be set apart as a separate Flathead reservation, and was not to be opened to settlement until the President decided.

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission found that the 12,005,000 acres ceded by this treaty were worth $5,300,000 on March 8, 1859, and that the $593,377.82 paid was unconscionable.

breaches.what: After a federal commission tried from 1896 to 1901 to obtain the tribes' agreement to cede part of the reservation and failed, Congress passed the Act of April 23, 1904 to allot the Flathead Reservation and sell the "surplus" land. The Court of Claims held the lands disposed of were taken within the meaning of the Fifth Amendment, found the diversion of proceeds to others inconsistent with a good faith effort to pay full value, and awarded $6,066,668.78 plus interest as part of just compensation.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Act of April 23, 1904, 33 Stat. 302, as found by the Court of Claims in Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes v. United States, 437 F.2d 458 (Ct. Cl. 1971)

breaches.what: An article in Char-Koosta News, the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes' newspaper, says Chief Victor defended the Bitterroot Valley as his people's homeland, that language differences caused misunderstandings about the treaty, and that the tribes were later forcibly, though not entirely, relocated to the Flathead Reservation.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Char-Koosta News, 'History: The Hellgate Treaty of 1855' (submitted by Patrick Matt)

source.title: History: The Hellgate Treaty of 1855
source.publisher: Char-Koosta News, Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes

landTaken: 12,005,000 acres ceded in 1855, including 55,000 acres of Flathead Lake (ICC Docket 61, 1965). The Court of Claims (1971) describes the reserved tract as some 1,245,000 acres, opened to settlement under the 1904 Act.
compensation: $4,431,622.18 final judgment for the 1855 cession (ICC, 1966). $6,066,668.78 plus interest as part of just compensation for lands disposed of under the 1904 Act (Court of Claims, 1971).
today: Not researched past the 1971 Court of Claims judgment.

nationVoice.summary: In the Tribes' newspaper, the treaty is described as a turning point that cost millions of acres, made under pressure and with misunderstandings, and followed by forced relocation from the Bitterroot.

openQuestions: Article 11 (the Bitterroot Valley) and the removal of the Bitterroot Salish to the Jocko reservation in 1891 were not traced to a finding in this pass; the 1872 Garfield agreement and its disputed signature should be researched.

The Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes' own website (cskt.org) blocked automated access; the nation's voice here comes from a submitted article in the Tribes' newspaper and should be replaced with an official CSKT account if one is available.
Whether the 1971 Court of Claims judgment was paid, and in what amount with interest, was not found.

Audit 2026-11-08: the 1966 final judgment changed from claims-commission to litigation, because it was entered on a compromise settlement (Docket 61, Final Judgment, August 5, 1966). The 1965 finding of unconscionable consideration stands.
Audit 2026-11-08: the 1904 breach reworded; the Court of Claims says the 1896-1901 efforts to secure the tribes' agreement "failed", not that the tribes refused.
